title: UN climate talks expose a just-transition dispute over finance and ambition
titleOriginal: The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words | Editorial
text: The Guardian argues that COP31’s breakdown exposed wealthy countries’ reluctance to pay and petrostates’ resistance to ambition, and that just transition needs more than rhetoric.

title: COP31 cover draft removes fossil-fuel and adaptation-finance specifics
text:
COP31’s third presidency draft drops direct fossil-fuel language and gives no clear timetable for tripling adaptation finance, a $120bn adaptation target, or the next IPCC report, showing an attempt to preserve the process while sidestepping the most binding political disputes.

Released on the eve of closure, the draft tests whether the presidency can convert dispute into an acceptable minimum consensus. It also follows earlier drafts that steadily stripped out finance and fossil-fuel provisions.

This is one of the formal COP31 cover-decision texts and sits directly inside the process that shapes the summit’s final political outcome.

title: Climate-finance work programme narrows to process language at COP31
titleOriginal: NEW: Slimmed-down climate finance text lands, with most substance gone
text:
At COP31, the climate-finance work programme was cut from 11 pages to 2, with burden-sharing, contributor-base expansion and tripling-adaptation-finance provisions removed, showing that parties are still contesting who should carry finance responsibility, how long the process should run, and what kind of outcome it should deliver.

The text emerged during the ministerial endgame, showing that the finance dispute had shifted from principle to line-by-line subtraction. It also helps explain why later cover-decision drafts continued to avoid finance substance.

This is a negotiation text for the COP31 climate-finance work programme and belongs to the formal process rather than external commentary.

title: Nature paper calls for mandatory water-footprint transparency in mining
titleOriginal: Accounting for the mining industry’s global water footprint
text:
The paper argues that mining firms’ withdrawals, discharges and contamination should be subject to mandatory disclosure, with transparency treated as a condition for capital allocation to critical-mineral supply chains, correcting the information gaps and externalized risks produced by voluntary reporting and fragmented regulation.

As critical-mineral supply chains expand, communities near extraction sites still have limited visibility over water risks, so the paper elevates transparency from a reporting issue to a financing condition.

The paper speaks to mining regulation, supply-chain due diligence and sustainable-finance frameworks; no formal negotiating submission is documented, but it directly bears on policy design for critical minerals and water governance.

title: Water-governance resilience depends on coordination and accountability
titleOriginal: Resilience as a governing principle in water governance
text:
Drawing on five international cases, the authors argue that resilience in water governance should not be treated as a static end state but as a governing principle, relying on adaptability, coordination, learning and accountability to manage cross-sector and cross-scale uncertainty.

As drought and flood risks rise and infrastructure vulnerability deepens, engineering capacity alone no longer explains why water systems fail or how they recover. The study offers a more institutional language for current debates over adaptation and implementation.

The paper speaks to water-governance reform and adaptation policy design; it is not embedded in a formal international negotiation text, but it is directly relevant to basin and urban water-management institutions.

title: Who Controls Multilateral Development Finance?
source: Rebecca Ray · Global Governance: A Review of Multilateralism and International Organizations
text:
The article measures voting-power distributions across 28 multilateral development banks and distinguishes creditor-led, core borrower-led, and mutual aid-oriented governance types. It shows that who holds governance power is closely tied to who can shape the direction and terms of development finance.

The author uses Penrose-Banzhaf and Shapley-Shubik power indices, together with members’ relative voting power on MDB boards, to compare governance structures across 28 MDBs.

Read alongside this issue’s COP31 finance deadlock, because the recurring disputes over burden sharing, funding sources, and financing conditions all come back to who controls the money and who bears the costs.

How does MDB voting power affect the distribution of climate finance? multilateral development banks voting power climate finance burden sharing governance How do borrower countries gain greater influence in development finance governance? borrower-led governance MDB reform institutional power development finance representation

title: Legitimacy by Design: Institutional Representation and Public Support for Global Governance
source: Philipp Bien, Thomas Malang, Matthias Mader · International Studies Quarterly
text:
The study finds that including parliamentarians in international-organization decision-making significantly raises perceived legitimacy. The effect is especially strong among politically diverse or skeptical publics, making representational design a scalable institutional response to legitimacy pressure in global governance.

The authors use a pre-registered conjoint experiment in which respondents evaluate hypothetical IO decisions varying across several attributes, including the presence and type of parliamentary involvement. Comparing these scenarios allows them to estimate how representational design affects legitimacy perceptions.

Read alongside the post-COP31 debate on climate-governance reform: when negotiation machinery fails to produce consensus, this paper suggests legitimacy is built into institutional design itself, not added afterward.

Does broader representation ease legitimacy crises in global governance? global governance legitimacy representation parliamentarians conjoint experiment Which forms of institutional participation most increase public support? international organizations public support participation legitimacy institutional design

title: Investment claims may constrain clean-energy industrial policy
titleOriginal: Investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) mechanisms are threatening economic, energy and security priorities
text:
Investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) can put investment protection in tension with public-interest policy: claims may constrain governments’ ability to pursue industrial, security and domestic economic priorities during the clean-energy transition. This makes investment-law constraints relevant to assessing whether transition policies can be implemented.

Published on 4 November, the commentary connects investment-protection disputes to current clean-energy and industrial-policy priorities. Read alongside Brazil’s transition roadmap, it raises an implementation question: how much legal room do governments have to use the proposed policy tools?

This is an analytical contribution to debates about the compatibility of investment treaties and clean-transition policy. The available source does not establish a formal COP31 submission or an adopted rule.

title: Poorer households bear disproportionate disaster-related welfare losses
text:
Microsimulations across 132 countries find that the poorest populations bear 9% of asset damage but 33% of well-being losses. Asset-based accounting therefore understates their recovery burden; risk assessment and recovery funding should also consider consumption losses, coping capacity and support targeted at lower-income groups.

Published on 29 October, the study provides an analytical frame for this issue’s wildfire-recovery coverage: damage totals do not capture the full burden on survivors. It shifts attention towards which households recover more slowly and which forms of support deliver greater well-being gains.

The findings inform disaster-risk metrics, recovery finance and the distributional choices in development planning. These are policy applications of the research, not evidence that it has been placed on a formal negotiating agenda.

title: Counting Carbon or Counting Coal? Anchoring Climate Governance in Fossil Fuel–Based Accountability Frameworks
source: Fergus Green, Declan Kuch · Global Environmental Politics
text:
The article compares accountability frameworks based on fossil-fuel reserves, production and infrastructure. It identifies serious risks in reserve-based approaches and favours combining production and infrastructure measures, whose greater transparency can support public oversight and accountability for states’ climate performance.

The authors use a sociotechnical analysis of existing fossil-fuel monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) schemes. The abstract does not detail scheme selection or data-collection procedures.

Read alongside Brazil’s transition roadmap, the paper raises a practical question: which verifiable production or infrastructure indicators could make nationally tailored pathways accountable?

Are production-based metrics more accountable than reserve-based ones? fossil fuel accountability MRV production data climate governance How can transition roadmaps be turned into verifiable mechanisms? transition roadmap verification monitoring climate governance

title: Are the BRICS (Really) Shaping a New Approach to Global Governance?
source: Francesco Petrone · Global Governance: A Review of Multilateralism and International Organizations
text:
The author examines whether the BRICS can advance a more inclusive model of global governance, with climate change as the main focus. The argument recognises progress in reform but identifies internal divisions, reliance on legacy energy sources and uncertainty around expansion as constraints on a coherent alternative.

The paper uses a comparative and critical method to examine governance reform. The abstract does not specify case-selection or data-collection procedures.

Read alongside the IPCC funding and participation dispute, the paper offers a lens on representation and effectiveness in multilateral reform; it does not study this particular IPCC meeting.

How do internal differences affect collective capacity for governance reform? BRICS institutional reform collective action climate governance How can multilateral reform combine representation with effectiveness? multilateralism representation institutional effectiveness Global South

title: Interactive: Who wants what at the COP31 climate change summit
text:
Carbon Brief compiles around 100 documents to map how parties at COP31, under the Australia-Turkey joint presidency, line up on climate finance, just transition, mitigation, adaptation and the global stocktake, showing that the real contest has shifted from broad ambition to mechanism boundaries, financing conditions and issue linkage.

The Antalya conference is about to open, while war, an energy crisis and climate extremes are raising pressure for finance and implementation. It directly tests whether the post-COP30 promise of an “implementation COP” can be made real.

This is the agenda map for COP31 formal negotiations and the baseline text for positioning around the just transition mechanism, climate finance and the action agenda.

title: COP17: Key outcomes agreed at the UN biodiversity conference in Yerevan
text:
Carbon Brief argues that COP17 completed the first global review of progress toward the 2030 nature targets, but the “deep concern” outcome shows most of the 23 targets are still off track; funding gaps, disputes over who should contribute, and a nearly empty fund expose structural weaknesses in biodiversity governance around finance, monitoring and responsibility allocation.

This is the midpoint review of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, with just over four years left to 2030. Countries have signed the key texts, but the implementation gap has been put squarely on the table.

This is the post-COP17 outcome summary feeding directly into COP18 preparation and the midterm accountability process for the Global Biodiversity Framework.

title: The UK’s 2026 Autumn Budget has laid the ground for cleaner and cheaper electricity. The 2027 Spending Review must build on it
text:
E3G argues that the UK Autumn Budget has already accepted that policy costs should no longer sit on electricity bills and has opened a window for deeper electricity-market reform; if the 2027 Spending Review follows through, it can align lower bills, a cleaner power system and growth objectives.

Fiscal rules and electricity pricing are being reset, which will determine whether the new government stops at bill relief or advances a systemic redesign of the power market.

This is a pre-budget policy case for linking the 2027 Spending Review to electricity-market reform.

title: COP31 must bridge ambition and action as world leaders face risks from climate target overshoot
text:
E3G argues that COP31 must convert ambition into delivery: under rising economic and energy-security pressures, the summit should use just transition, finance and implementation arrangements to prevent target overshoot from hardening into governance failure.

The article sets three tests for COP31 in direct response to current debate over the negotiating agenda and the risk of target overshoot. It frames the summit as a delivery test rather than another declaration round.

This is a pre-COP31 framing document intended to shape agenda setting and success criteria.

title: Challenges of the OECD’s Tax Governance Regime Leading to the United Nations’ ‘(Re)entry’ into International Tax Law Governance
source: Jonathan R. Everhart · Global Governance: A Review of Multilateralism and International Organizations
text:
The article argues that although the OECD-led GloBE rules created an inclusive framework, the governance and rule-making process still favors member states, making the arrangement insufficiently beneficial for developing countries; it therefore proposes a stronger UN role in international tax governance and a UN High-level Political Forum on International Taxation.

The article uses institutional analysis to compare the inclusiveness and distributive effects of OECD governance arrangements with those under the UN; the available abstract does not specify a quantitative method.

Read alongside Carbon Brief’s COP31 coverage to see how multilateral rule-making faces similar disputes over procedural inclusion in climate finance and just transition.

Why is tax governance returning to the UN? international tax governance UN tax forum OECD GloBE Global South How does inclusiveness shape rule allocation? global governance institutional legitimacy rule-making power OECD United Nations

title: National Institutions and Global Public Goods: Are Democracies More Cooperative in Climate Change Policy?
source: Michèle B. Bättig, Thomas Bernauer · International Organization
text:
The article tests whether democracies provide more global public goods and finds that democratic states make stronger climate policy commitments, but emissions outcomes are not consistently better; domestic institutions can raise policy output without necessarily overcoming free-riding, discounting and sectoral constraints such as transport.

The authors use cross-sectional data for 185 countries from 1990 to 2004 to compare democracy levels with climate policy commitments and emissions outcomes.

Read alongside this week’s E3G item on the UK budget and electricity-market reform, which also grapples with the gap between policy commitments and real-world emissions or price outcomes.

When do domestic institutions translate into emissions cuts? democracy climate policy policy output emissions outcomes Why do commitments and outcomes diverge? global public goods free-riding climate governance transport sector

title: Chart: A record two-thirds of car sales in China are now electric vehicles
text:
Using China Passenger Car Association data, Carbon Brief shows that new-energy vehicles reached 67% of new car sales in September 2026, indicating that electrification is shifting from subsidy-led expansion toward self-reinforcing market growth and now affects global auto trade and oil demand through exports and transport substitution.

The shift comes after the Hormuz crisis raised fuel costs, suggesting that external energy shocks are accelerating transport electrification rather than merely causing temporary disruption. The September 2026 sales data provide the latest window into a structural turn in China’s auto market.

This sits at the intersection of China’s transport electrification agenda, changing oil demand, and export competition in the auto industry.

title: Experts: How are climate scientists using artificial intelligence?
text:
By assembling expert views, Carbon Brief shows that AI is now being used in weather prediction, satellite-image analysis and climate-policy support, but its energy demand, weak verifiability and tendency to widen scientific inequalities imply that research institutions need validation standards, energy constraints and equitable access rules at the same time.

The AI boom is rapidly entering climate-science workflows; without method checks and allocation rules, gains in performance may come with new bias and inequality. The piece responds to this governance gap at the moment of expansion.

This sits at the intersection of climate-science methods, research governance and policy-tool deployment.

title: Climate may have slipped down the Annual Meetings agenda, but remains on the balance sheet
text:
E3G argues that climate may have receded from the main stage at the Bangkok IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings, but energy insecurity, extreme weather and fiscal pressure still keep climate risk on governments’ balance sheets, so multilateral development banks and finance tools must embed preventive adaptation investment and rapid post-shock support in routine financial arrangements.

The piece uses the Annual Meetings window to show climate being recoded by fiscal and risk-management logic rather than just by agenda rhetoric. It responds directly to current constraints on sovereign finance and adaptation investment.

This sits at the intersection of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings, development finance and the mainstreaming of climate risk.

title: EU ETS – Foundation for a Green Steel Ecosystem
text:
E3G argues that the EU Emissions Trading System can support green steel only if it is paired with complementary legislation, demand-side signals and industrial policy; otherwise pioneering projects will not become financeable, replicable low-carbon capacity and the transition will remain fragmented.

Europe is moving heavy-industry decarbonization from pilots to system-building, making the adequacy of the carbon-price, regulatory and market-building mix a live issue. The piece recasts the ETS as institutional foundation rather than a stand-alone abatement tool.

This sits at the intersection of EU industrial decarbonization, carbon-market design and competitiveness policy.

title: Multilateral Climate Finance in Pursuit of Private Capital: How the De-Risking Agenda Is Changing International Organizations
source: Erin R. Graham, Jiayi (Sonia) Zhang · Global Environmental Politics
text:
The article argues that multilateral climate finance is being reshaped by a de-risking agenda: international organizations increasingly use multilateral funds to mobilize institutional investors and domestic banks rather than finance individual mitigation or adaptation projects, blurring the line between economic and environmental IOs and creating transparency problems.

The authors combine text analysis of replenishment documents from five climate-finance international organizations with an assessment of GEF and GCF projects to compare how de-risking changes funding use and organizational roles.

Read alongside E3G’s "Climate may have slipped down the Annual Meetings agenda, but remains on the balance sheet" to see how adaptation and risk finance are being rewritten into multilateral financial rules.

Who benefits from de-risking in multilateral climate finance? multilateral climate finance de-risking institutional investors transparency How does de-risking reshape climate-finance allocation? GCF GEF financial intermediation climate projects

title: Theorizing Access in Global Environmental Governance: A Critical Analysis of COP26 and the COVID-19 Pandemic
source: Lauren M. Baker, Diana K. Elhard, Kimberly R. Marion Suiseeya, Laura Zanotti, Margaret O’Connell, Alexandra Anderson · Global Environmental Politics
text:
The article argues that access in global environmental governance cannot be reduced to attendance or open registration; collaborative event ethnography at COP26 shows that discriminatory design, technological disparities and recognitional injustice obstruct sustained, meaningful participation and deepen power asymmetries.

The authors use collaborative event ethnography at COP26 and draw on critical disability studies to rethink the differences among access, accessibility and inclusion.

Read with this issue’s COP17 biodiversity process stories and Inside Climate News’s "Battleground Ballots" to see how accessibility and political mobilization jointly shape governance outcomes.

How does conference accessibility affect negotiation outcomes? global environmental governance accessibility COP participation How do technological barriers amplify inequality in climate diplomacy? digital inequality inclusion conference participation disability studies

title: COP17: Which countries have released new pledges to tackle nature loss?
text:
Carbon Brief shows that 113 parties have now submitted updated NBSAPs, yet the Kunming-Montreal 2030 targets remain well off track; the central issue is not whether pledges exist, but whether they enter a comparable, trackable, and reviewable global process linked to finance, monitoring, and national reporting.

This analysis lands on the COP17 global review window, when countries will be assessed on updated commitments toward the 2030 targets. The original deadline has already been widely missed, so the gap between submission and implementation is now the negotiation’s core problem.

Direct input into the COP17 global review and the implementation agenda under the Kunming-Montreal framework.

title: COP17: Tracking progress towards the UN’s 2030 nature targets
text:
By tracking all 23 targets one by one, Carbon Brief argues that the bottleneck in nature governance has shifted from having a framework to knowing which targets are actually advancing, and the fact that 22 targets are off track shows that finance, subsidy reform, restoration, and monitoring still lack institutional coherence; the piece effectively argues for putting budgets, accountability, and implementation timing on the same ledger.

Published just before COP17, it provides the first global map of where progress is lagging by target. It challenges broad-brush claims and forces negotiators to confront the distribution of implementation failures.

Technical background for the COP17 progress review and the text negotiations that follow.

title: Explained: Reforms to the IMF and World Bank’s debt framework send a new climate signal – adaptation counts
text:
E3G argues that after the IMF and World Bank revised the Low-Income Countries Debt Sustainability Framework, debt assessments now take climate vulnerability and adaptation investment more seriously, meaning multilateral financial rules are beginning to treat adaptation not as an extra cost but as part of debt realism and development resilience.

This explainer responds to policy changes around the 2026 annual meetings, showing that the debt framework is no longer a purely fiscal tool but now absorbs climate risk. It offers an institutional entry point for adaptation finance.

Policy interpretation of the revised MDB and IMF debt framework, part of the post-annual-meetings implementation agenda.

title: The BRICS Sustainability Paradox in Global Governance
source: Hendry Roris P. Sianturi, Uud Wahyudin, Budi Nugraha, Reddy Anggara · Global Governance: A Review of Multilateralism and International Organizations
text:
The authors argue that ‘green growth’ and ‘responsible tourism’ in the BRICS often function as legitimacy performance rather than structural transformation; the communication–implementation gap shows that sustainability language can mask continuity unless independent verification, impact-based metrics, and Southern epistemologies are brought in.

This is a Global Forum-style conceptual analysis that uses tourism as the lens for examining the sustainability gap in governance.

Read alongside this week’s Carbon Brief coverage of COP17 pledges and UN News reporting from Armenia, since both ask how commitments become verifiable implementation.

How do Southern epistemologies alter verification of sustainability pledges? Southern epistemologies verification global governance sustainability metrics Why does tourism magnify the implementation gap in sustainability governance? tourism governance implementation gap legitimacy global governance

title: Democratization, International Knowledge Institutions, and Global Governance
text:
The author argues that international knowledge institutions constrain power in global governance by setting standards for reasoning and deliberation, classifying objects of international discourse, and shaping participation; knowledge production itself therefore requires democratic critique.

This is a theory-driven article offering normative and conceptual analysis of the functions of international knowledge institutions.

Read alongside this issue’s two Carbon Brief COP17 pieces, since both deal with how targets, indicators, and reporting shape governance power.

How do indicators shape power in global environmental governance? indicators knowledge institutions global governance accountability Who gets to define compliance standards in international regimes? compliance standards participation international institutions
